results.summary_before: This is a minimal perceptron-based branch predictor that reads branch instruction addresses and ground truth directions via SPI and outputs predictions. It is based on a research paper and uses latch-based memory, with a functional simulation in C++ and CocoTB tests. It requires external hardware to drive inputs and read outputs, and is notable for its use of a perceptron model and detailed debugging features.
results.summary: This is a 16-bit simple processor with UART receive and transmit data pins and baud-rate selection inputs. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the instruction set, architecture, or internal blocks. UART communication is emulated within the testbench, and no external hardware is required. The design has been resubmitted on multiple shuttle runs but has no silicon test reports.

results.summary_before: This design produces siren-like tones and light patterns reminiscent of 1970s effects, using a chain of D flip-flops to divide the clock into various frequencies. Higher frequencies generate tones for audio output, while lower frequencies control the patterns on a seven-segment display and modulate the tones. A pattern select input chooses between two groups of patterns. External hardware such as a speaker with a series resistor or an audio amplifier is required for sound output.
results.summary: This is a phase/frequency detector that compares a reference clock and a feedback clock and outputs the phase difference on up and inverted down pins. It is described as one of the blocks of a phase locked loop. If the feedback clock leads the reference, the up signal shows the phase difference; if it lags, the down signal shows the difference. External signal generators are required for the square wave inputs.

results.summary_before: Convertidor de Tiempo a Digital (TDC) is a time-to-digital converter that measures the width of an input pulse and transmits the digital value via RS232. It includes a counter, a state machine, and an RS232 transmitter operating at 9600 baud with odd parity. The design is intended for interfacing with time-output sensors and was tested in simulation and on an FPGA development board.
results.summary: This is a trivial self-timed logic example implementing an LFSR using dual redundant encoding to distinguish data and null states. The documentation is incomplete and notes that testing requires a scope and a way to drive inputs. A partial silicon test report states that the single C-gate works as expected, but the oscillator goes to a constant value when init is asserted. The author expected more randomness from the oscillator.

results.summary_before: This design implements a register bank that can be accessed through either an SPI or an I2C serial interface, with a digital input selecting which interface is active. It is used by writing and reading registers over the selected bus, and the first register is documented as controlling LEDs on the demo board. External hardware may include 2k2 pull-up resistors on the I2C SDA and SCL lines, and testers have used a Bus Pirate and a Pico with internal pull-ups to exercise both interfaces. Silicon tests confirmed read and write access over SPI and I2C, including multi-byte transfers and cross-interface access to the same registers.
results.summary: This design uses manually instantiated inverter cells to form a configurable ring oscillator with selectable chain lengths, expected to oscillate from about 15 MHz up to 350 MHz. The selected clock drives a worker counter that counts up to 3000, and a VGA sync generator takes pixel color from the upper six bits of the counter. The counter is reset during the horizontal blanking interval of each VGA line, producing vertical colored bars with some jitter. A silicon test report confirmed working VGA output and a ring oscillator frequency of about 78 MHz.

results.summary: This design counts until the heat death of the universe and broadcasts the counter value every second over 100Mbps Ethernet. It reuses the Teapot Ethernet accelerator wrapper for full-duplex communication over a CAT-3/5 cable. The ASIC autonomously sends an application packet with ethertype 0x88b5 every second. External hardware includes an Ethernet 100BASE-T PMOD connector with a LAN8720A PHY and a 50 MHz oscillator.
